offending.as_cited: Xiang Fu Ji v City of New York (13 NY3d 791, 794)
offending.cited_case_name: Xiang Fu Ji v City of New York
offending.quoted_text: construed liberally to effectuate its remedial purpose
offending.court_quote: On two occasions, the plaintiff's brief purported to quote the nonexistent Court of Appeals case of Xiang Fu Ji v City of New York (13 NY3d 791, 794) for the proposition that Administrative Code of the City of New York § 7-210 … is a remedial statute that should be “construed liberally to effectuate its remedial purpose.” No case by that title exists at all, much less at the citation given by the plaintiff's brief.
offending.what_actually_exists: A real Court of Appeals case, Xiang Fu He v Troon Mgt., Inc. (34 NY3d 167), analyses Administrative Code § 7-210, but it does not contain the purported quotation. The Court of Appeals has actually held the opposite — that § 7-210, in derogation of the common law, “must be strictly construed” (Vucetovic v Epsom Downs, Inc., 10 NY3d 517, 521).

offending.quoted_text: in the best position to monitor and control
offending.court_quote: The plaintiff's brief also contained a fictitious quote from the fictitious case of Hausser v Giunta (88 AD3d 969, 970). The plaintiff's brief on two occasions quoted that fictitious case as stating that Administrative Code § 7-210 shifted liability for sidewalk defects from the City to abutting property owners, who are “in the best position to monitor and control” the condition of adjacent walkways.
offending.what_actually_exists: There is a real Hausser v Giunta (217 AD2d 604, revd 88 NY2d 449) concerning sidewalk liability, but it arose in the City of Long Beach under City of Long Beach Code § 256 rather than Administrative Code § 7-210, and it does not contain the quotation.

offending.court_quote: The final fictitious citation in the plaintiff's brief is to the fictitious case of Lack v Lack (841 NYS2d 403, 404), which the plaintiff's brief cited for the proposition that this Court reviews a grant of summary judgment de novo, applying the same standards as the trial court. Again, no case by that name appears at that citation, and there appears to have never been any cases in New York with that title.
offending.what_actually_exists: Nothing. No New York case has ever borne that title.

offending.as_cited: Campaign for Fiscal Equity v State of New York (86 NY2d 307, 318)
offending.cited_case_name: Campaign for Fiscal Equity v State of New York
offending.court_quote: The plaintiff's brief cited Campaign for Fiscal Equity v State of New York (86 NY2d 307, 318) for the proposition that exceptions to remedial statutes should be strictly construed. … The opinion in Campaign for Fiscal Equity does not use the words remedial or exception, or discuss how strictly statutes should be construed. The pin cite given in the plaintiff's brief refers to a section of the opinion discussing the standard for considering the sufficiency of a pleading on a motion pursuant to CPLR 3211(a)(7).
offending.what_actually_exists: Campaign for Fiscal Equity v State of New York, 86 NY2d 307, is a real Court of Appeals decision about public school financing; page 318 discusses the CPLR 3211(a)(7) pleading standard.

offending.as_cited: Rodgers v. City of New York, 34 A.D.3d 555 (2d Dep't 2006)
offending.cited_case_name: Rodgers v City of New York
offending.quoted_text: [w]hile Rodgers v. City of New York, 34 A.D.3d 555 (2d Dep't 2006), held that a two-year search can be sufficient, that holding is not a blanket rule applicable in all circumstances.
offending.court_quote: However, Rodgers concerned only a motion by an adjacent landowner, and not the City, and did not address the issue of prior written notice or how long a time frame a municipality must search its records in order to establish the lack of prior written notice (see Rodgers v City of New York, 34 AD3d 555, 555-556). In other words, Rodgers said nothing remotely related to whether a two-year search can be sufficient.
offending.what_actually_exists: Rodgers v City of New York, 34 AD3d 555, is a real Second Department decision, but it concerned a motion by an adjacent landowner and says nothing about prior written notice or record-search periods.
